name: Rosa Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Rosa, and thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say is confidential. Can you tell me what a normal working day looks like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a blast-hole drill at the Cerro Blanco lithium mine, out on the salt flats about forty minutes from town. The rig sits on tracks and I drill rows of holes, fifteen metres deep, to a pattern the engineers send to my screen, so the blasting crew can charge them. I'm the slowest driller on the bench, I'll tell you that straight, but I'm getting there. What I love is the morning, when the flats are pink and there's nobody but me and the rig. What wears me out is the wind, and the fact that I'm fifty-eight learning something the others learned at twenty.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up drilling at fifty-six?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a care worker for twenty years and then I drove the school bus, and both paid nothing. When the lithium boom came the company ran a programme for older workers and women, so I applied. My partner Luis has bad lungs from welding and gets a small disability pension, and we spent our savings helping our daughter through her divorce last year. So we're starting from almost zero. I use the AI on my phone every day, by the way, to study the drill manuals and to check my maths on the patterns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Honestly, I'd be a little sorry, because the AI on my phone is half my teacher. But a quiet few years would let me become a good driller instead of a slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the union newsletter I'd write that the plateau gives us breathing room, so let's use it for training, not for sitting still. I'd say the drills on trial down the road at Salar Norte are still coming, hype or no hype. And I'd tell the women on the bench to go for their tickets now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the plateau suits me: AI stays my study helper and I get time to catch up. What I can't shake is the money, because we spent everything on our daughter's divorce and Luis's pension barely covers his medicines. One bad month, a car repair or short shifts after a lithium price dip, and we're borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the next drill ticket within a year, which is about 140 more a week. I'd keep studying the manuals with the AI every evening. And once the ticket comes through, I'd put the first thirty a week into a jar for Luis's medicines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the hopeful direction. The work's all right; it's the bank balance that keeps me honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at the mine if the lithium price dips?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last time, two years ago, they cut every crew to four-day weeks for three months. On my pay a four-day week is the gas bill gone. The young ones grumbled, and I did sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Luis worry about your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis worries that I'm fifty-eight and climbing onto a drill rig in the wind. My partner Luis says he married a care worker and somehow ended up with a miner. I tell him the rig is easier on my back than lifting old men ever was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the engineers' side goes first, the drill patterns and the planning. My side, sitting on the rig, waits a bit. But the drill already does half of it by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the newsletter I'd write that the company has to train us for the remote operations centre now, while there's time, and older workers shouldn't be last in line. I'd say the drills on trial at Salar Norte are robots, and robots are slow in this picture, but slow isn't never. I'd want retraining written into the next agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is drilling to a pattern a computer sends me, so I'm already mostly a babysitter for the rig. When the pattern design goes to AI and the trial drills prove themselves, one person in a room can watch six rigs. I'd want to be that person, but with zero savings I can't afford a single week of unpaid training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the training office about the remote operations centre in the first week and sign up for anything they offer. I'd study automation basics at night with the AI, which I'm half doing already. And I'd push the union to make retraining on full pay a right, because people like me can't learn for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. I'm good at learning, and I'm frightened of running out of time and money before it counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the bench would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dolores, who started the same month as me and hates screens. Dolores is sixty and drills better than I do, but she'd be lost in a control room. I'd want her in the union's training group, sitting next to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your hours were trimmed while you trained?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, by selling it and taking the mine bus. Then my phone plan, though I'd keep the AI, because that's my teacher. Luis's medicines don't get cut, ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. So the screen jobs go first. That's the ones I was aiming for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the newsletter I'd write that the remote operations centre is not a safe harbour any more, because that's thinking work and it goes in 2028. I'd say the hands-on jobs, maintenance, fitting, fixing the rigs, are the ones with three more years. And I'd say the company should train us for those now, on full pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think my whole plan just turned upside down. I was going to sit at screens because my hands are slow, and now the screens are the first thing gone. Worse, the autonomous drills are already on trial down the road, so mine might not even wait for 2031. I'd be 60 with no savings and Luis on a disability pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch straight away from the remote centre to the maintenance crew, and ask to shadow the fitters on my days off. I'd use the AI every night to learn hydraulics and the drill's electrics, because that's hands-on work that lasts a bit longer. We'd sell the car and I'd get the mine bus, which saves about sixty a week. And I'd organise in the union for retraining on full pay, not a leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest, and a bit angry. I'm good at learning, but I'm learning toward a door that's closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the fitters would take you on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Benny on the maintenance crew already lets me hand him spanners on night shift. He says I ask too many questions, which from Benny is a compliment. But they'd need fitters for three years and then not at all, so it's a short bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen at home if the drill job went in 2029 or 2030?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis's pension pays for his medicine and not much else. We'd have to ask our daughter for a room, and she's only just back on her feet after the divorce. I'm quick to learn, but I can't learn my way out of having nothing in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 and 2034. Now that's a timeline I can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the newsletter I'd say we've got five years before the screen jobs change and eight before the hands-on ones do, so there's no excuse for the company not training us. I'd push for a proper training fund. I'd want the older workers first in line, not last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right in this one. I'd be 63 when the computers come and 66 when the robots do, so I could do a diploma, work as a fitter for a few good years and retire before the robots reach the workshop. The only thing I'd worry about is the drills on trial nearby moving faster than the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol in a two-year night diploma in mechanical maintenance at the technical college, about 900 a year, and use AI as my tutor. I'd get the next drill ticket first so the extra 140 a week pays for it. And I'd save around thirty a week once the ticket comes through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. I like a project, and this one has an end date I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: 900 a year with no savings. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The next drill ticket pays for it, more or less. If the union wins a training fund, even better. I'd rather owe the college than owe nobody and know nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else would you want to bring along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The women from the programme, there are six of us who started late. Give me five years and a laptop and I'll be the oldest fitter on the salt flats. I'd want the other five beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039? I'd be seventy-one. I'd be retired and nagging Luis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the picture for the young drillers, and the union should start the training fund now for them. Ten years is plenty if someone starts the clock. I'd write that in the newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd retire before either date, and my worry would move to my grandkids. I'm not racing the robots in this one, I'm just making sure they don't drive off with my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my next drill ticket, then start saving properly for the first time in years. I'd run an evening AI class for older workers at the union hall, because I'm already the one everyone asks. And I'd keep drilling till my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little sorry I won't see the cool part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean, making sure they don't drive off with your pension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pension fund owns shares in mining companies. If robots make the company rich and the workers poor, I want the pension fund to get its slice. With ten years I'm not racing the robots anymore, I'm just making sure they don't drive off with my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teach a class if you're retiring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like it, and because when I started at fifty-six nobody taught me anything slowly. An older worker who learns the AI at the union hall gets an extra few years at the mine. That's worth an evening a week.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the screen jobs I was aiming for go first and the drills soon after, and being clever doesn't help if there's no time. What would help is a training fund that pays you while you learn, not after, and a basic income floor so people like Luis and me don't fall through. Paid for by whoever owns the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but there are people breathing silica dust on the drills right now. If a robot can take the dust instead of my lungs, I want it, I just want my wage to come with me.

headlineQuote: If a robot can take the dust instead of my lungs, I want it, I just want my wage to come with me.
portrait: Rosa Nakamura, 58, drills **blast holes** at the Cerro Blanco lithium mine after twenty years in care work.
She and Luis, who has **a small disability pension**, spent their savings helping their daughter last year.
She uses AI every day; in a plateau she's **uneasy**, hopeful about the job but with no money for a bad month.
Steady change makes her **anxious**: AI takes the drill planning, and she can't afford unpaid retraining.
AGI by 2028 **alarms** her; with five or ten years she'd train as a fitter and retire before the robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the screen jobs she'd aim for go first and the drills soon after.
Being **a quick learner** wouldn't matter without time.
whatWouldHelp: A **training fund** that pays people while they learn.
A **basic income floor**, paid for by whoever owns the robots.
